new_statements.quote: In contexts where new information is given or a word is relatively important in its context, a pragmatic prominence tends to be placed on the final syllable of a phonological word (though with the exception of certain enclitic clause-final markers such as =os ‘CFM:SOFT’ if present; see section 3.3 below). [...] Given this bias toward monosyllables, identifying word-level features such as stress is less than straightforward, since if the vast majority of words in a clause are monosyllabic, and every word has lexical stress, there will be no meaningful contrast in lexical stress for most of that clause.
new_statements.citation: White, Nathan M. 2021. The Hmong Language of North Queensland. PhD thesis, James Cook University. doi:10.25903/f5rd-s089. (Covers White Hmong and Green Mong / Mong Leng; the passage is about Hmong generally, examples from White Hmong speakers.)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (text). Both quoted sentences are there verbatim: 'In contexts where new information is given.. see section 3.3 below).' is the opening of sect. 2.8 'Pragmatic prominences' on printed p. 70 (PDF page 107; lines 4871-4880). 'Given this bias toward monosyllables.. for most of that clause.' is in sect. 3.1 'Phonological word' ( lines 5262-5266) -- but on printed p. 79 (PDF page 116, header '79'), not p. 80 as the locator says; the final entry for hmon1264 already has p. 79 and 'printed = PDF page minus 37'. Sect. 3.1.1 heading is on p. 80 (PDF 117) and the 'iambic-like pattern' passage with fn. 25 on p. 81 (PDF 118), examples continuing on p. 82, so 'pp. 80-82' is fine. Only the one pag…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Seven-tone language; no lexical (contrastive) word stress is posited. When a word is new or important, an optional pragmatic prominence falls on the FINAL syllable of the phonological word (an iambic-like pattern in polysyllables: longer duration, greater intensity, wider pitch range on the final syllable, compression of non-final syllables). Supporting second-hand note: Mortensen 2006 (UC Berkeley diss., p. 247, Mong Leng data) says 'Hmong has (according to the available evidence) iambic stress and right-headed prosodic constituents'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. White 2021 sect. 2.9 describes a separate intensification process (vowel lengthening / raised pitch) on the first non-reduplicated syllable, and four-syllable elaborate expressions may carry prominences on syllables 2 and 4 (sect. 3.1.1).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic clause-final markers such as =os never take the prominence (it lands on the preceding syllable); English loanwords replace English stress with tone (stressed syllable -> /55/ or /33/, unstressed -> /22/) rather than showing the iambic pattern (p. 66-67, fn. 21, fn. 25).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (the prominence is White's main diagnostic of wordhood); it is optional and pragmatically conditioned, absent in careful slow speech and in rapid speech. Clause-level emphatic prominence (vowel lengthening, tone raising on time/locative phrases) is described separately by Kunyot 1984 sect. 2.4.3 p. 33 for Hmong Njua of Ban Khek Noi, Thailand.
new_statements.identity_note: hmon1338 is Glottolog's Bookkeeping entry for the RETIRED ISO 639-3 code [blu] 'Hmong Njua'. ISO CR 2007-188 split [blu] into hnj (Hmong Njua / Mong Leng / Green Mong = Glottolog hmon1264), cqd (Chuanqiandian Cluster Miao, chua1256), hrm (Horned Miao, horn1235), sfm (Small Flowery Miao) and an update of hmn. Every descriptive source that used the name 'Hmong Njua' / 'Mong Njua' / 'Mong Leng' / 'Green Mong' (Lyman 1974, 1979; Kunyot 1984; Harriehausen 1990; Mortensen 2004, 2006, 2019; White 2021, 2025) describes hmon1264, which is ALREADY in the catalog (classification tonal-OR-pitch accent, source White 2021). Under the code-currency rule (a retired code does not make a separate language) hmon1338 should be merged into / redirected to hmon1264, not entered as a second language. The statement quoted below is from the same on-disk White 2021 file that hmon1264 already cites (White covers White Hmong hmon1333 and Green Mong hmon1264 together, as spoken in North Queensland).

sources.note: Tagmemic syntax; sect. 1.9 Transcription (pp. 7-11) follows Lyman 1970 (consonants, vowels, 7 tones), no stress remark, and says 'more study of the Hmong Njua phonology should be done'. Sect. 2.4.3 'Other prominence' p. 33: 'Elements in a clause may be given increased prominence by lengthening the vowel and/or raising the tones of those elements. Elements which are usually given prominence are time and locative phrases' -- clause-level emphasis, not word stress. downloaded from the Internet Archive copy 2021-01-24 of sealang.net/archives/mahidol/sealang.net itself down, expired certificate).
